summary: This Standards Track document defines transport mechanisms for moving CMC messages: HTTP, file, mail, and TCP. It obsoletes RFC 5273 and RFC 6402.

eli5.summary: It lists the ways to deliver the certificate paperwork: web, files, email, or a direct connection.

subtitle: How certificate requests and responses travel between clients and a certificate authority: over HTTP, as files, by mail, or over raw TCP.

tldr.problem: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) defines the messages used to request and issue certificates, but those messages still need an agreed way to be carried between a client and a server.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines four transports: file-based, mail-based (MIME), HTTP using POST, and plain TCP on port 5318. Each one fixes the content types, file extensions or framing to use.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that replaces RFC 5273 and RFC 6402, folds in the TCP port assignment and tightens the TLS and HTTP rules. HTTP is expected to remain the main transport.

today: RFC 10003 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. It obsoletes RFC 5273 and RFC 6402, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
CMC messages are defined in a separate document, RFC 10002 (the CMC specification). This RFC only says how to move those messages around. The transport mechanisms it describes are HTTP, file, mail and TCP.

It obsoletes RFC 5273 and RFC 6402, and it also incorporates an erratum (number 3593) against RFC 5273. The usual RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 meaning of MUST and SHOULD applies when the words appear in capitals.

CMC distinguishes Simple PKI messages (a plain PKCS #10 request, and a response that only carries certificates) from Full PKI messages. Most of the transport rules differ depending on which of the two is being carried.
sections.eli5: Think of a letter and the different ways to deliver it. The letter's contents are described elsewhere. This document only explains the delivery routes.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 5273 and RFC 6402
sections.content:
This is a merge-and-tighten revision. The text of RFC 6402 was merged in, and IANA assigned TCP port 5318 for CMC. The file extensions for Full PKI Requests and Responses were clarified, and examples of encoding types for mail-based requests and responses were added.

  • TLS 1.0 was replaced by TLS 1.2 or later, and implementations are required to follow the recommendations in BCP 195.
  • HTTP guidance now points to RFC 9205.
  • Early data (0-RTT) is restricted when TLS 1.3 or QUIC is used.
  • The use of TCP pipelining is restricted.
  • The limits of SMTP-over-TLS and the use of authenticated TLS for message delivery were clarified.
sections.eli5: It is a cleaned-up second edition. Old, weak security settings were dropped, a fixed phone number (port) was added for the direct connection, and a few confusing parts were spelled out.

sections.title: The File-Based Protocol
sections.content:
Files suit cases such as enrolling an offline client. When a file carries a Full PKI Request or Response, it MUST hold exactly one message and the file MUST be binary encoded.

The document says the following file extensions SHOULD be used. The abbreviations crq and crp stand for Full PKI Request and Response.

  • Simple PKI Request: .p10
  • Full PKI Request: .crq
  • Simple PKI Response: .p7c
  • Full PKI Response: .crp
sections.eli5: Put one form in one folder-file, and give the file a name ending that tells people what kind of form it is.

sections.title: The Mail-Based Protocol
sections.content:
Mail uses MIME wrapping, taken from the S/MIME specification (RFC 8551). Unlike standard S/MIME, MIME wrapping between the layers of Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) wrapping is optional here.

Each message type has its own content type:

  • A Simple PKI Request uses application/pkcs10 (RFC 5967), and the file name extension MUST be .p10.
  • A Simple PKI Response uses application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type=certs-only and a .p7c file name.
  • A Full PKI Request uses application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type=CMC-Request and a .p7m file name.
  • A Full PKI Response uses application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type=CMC-Response and a .p7m file name.

The file name MUST appear in the name parameter of Content-Type or the filename parameter of Content-Disposition. Non-ASCII text is prohibited in these names. The RFC's example messages are deliberately truncated.
sections.eli5: For email, you stick a label on the envelope saying what is inside (request or answer, simple or full) and give the attachment a matching file name.

sections.title: The HTTP-Based Protocol
sections.content:
This is the transport the RFC expects to be used most. Clients are configured with enough information to form the server URI, and they submit requests with the POST method. Servers MUST use 2XX response codes for successful responses.

Clients MAY try HTTPS. If TLS is used by the HTTP version in play, the implementation MUST follow BCP 195. CMC implementations that support TLS 1.3 or QUIC MUST NOT use early data (0-RTT), because POST is not idempotent. Clients are not required to support HTTP authentication or cookies, so servers cannot rely on them.

For a request, the Content-Type MUST have the value from the MIME table, for example application/pkcs7-mime; smime-type=CMC-Request; name=request.p7m, and the body is the binary encoding of the PKI Request. A response body is the binary BER encoding of a Simple or Full PKI Response, with smime-type=CMC-Response and name=response.p7m in the example given.
sections.eli5: It works like submitting a web form: the client sends the paperwork in a POST, and the server answers with a success code and the reply paperwork.

sections.title: The TCP-Based Protocol and Its Port
sections.content:
Over TCP no wrapping is needed. Messages are sent in their binary encoded form. After a response, the client either closes the connection or sends another request on the same connection. Reusing one connection for several successive requests is RECOMMENDED, but the client MUST wait for the full response before sending the next request. A server MAY close an idle connection, typically after several minutes.

The service name is pkix-cmc and the TCP port is 5318, which IANA has assigned for CMC. Before RFC 6402, CMC had no registered port and used a port from the Private Port range. Clients MAY keep doing that, while a TCP server SHOULD use 5318. IANA also updated the smime-type registry entries for CMC-Request and CMC-Response to point to this document.

The document says it is expected that HTTP will continue to be the primary transport method used by CMC installations.
sections.eli5: The direct connection has its own numbered door, 5318. Send one request, wait for the whole answer, and then you can send the next one through the same door.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Replay protection may be needed depending on the environment. If the certification authority keeps a lot of state, replays may be detectable without the optional senderNonce and recipientNonce attributes, but developers of state-constrained PKI clients are strongly encouraged to use them.

Setting up a secure channel between a client and a CA or RA needs an out-of-band trust initiation step, which this document leaves out of scope. When no trust exists yet, for example while downloading trust anchors, the EnvelopedData or AuthEnvelopedData content types give the same shrouding that TLS would.

For mail, SMTP-over-TLS may protect only the first hop, so later relay hops may be neither authenticated nor encrypted. REQUIRETLS (RFC 8689) can request authenticated TLS at every hop, but risks non-delivery if a server on the path does not support it. For files, filesystem permissions can limit read access to the authorized user or group.
sections.eli5: Protect the paperwork on its trip. Sealing it in an envelope that only the right person can open works everywhere, even when the road itself is not safe.
